title: Pan American Fire & Casualty Co. v. Revere
lead: An insurer facing claims from a fatal school-bus collision sought one proceeding to allocate a policy too small to cover the anticipated demands.

actors.name: Accident claimants, including John Wells
actors.role: Competing potential recipients of limited insurance proceeds

proceedings: Insurer filed interpleader and deposited a $100,400 bond.
District court denied dismissal and granted statutory interpleader, directing claims, injunctions, and a jury process.
limits: This threshold historical order did not determine negligence or damages. Its broad injunction included the insured; the account does not assert validity under later precedent. Venue and service discussion uses 1960 rules.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent primary-source audit claimed.

sections.title: Two collisions generate claims against one policy
paragraphs: On February 3, 1960, a tractor-trailer collided head-on with a school bus near Covington, Louisiana. The bus driver and three children died, and twenty-three people were injured. A second collision among following vehicles injured John Wells.

The tractor’s insurer, Pan American Fire & Casualty, faced three filed suits and numerous additional claims against a $100,000 policy. It sought interpleader against potential claimants, restrictions on other proceedings, and adjudication in one action, depositing a $100,400 bond; the additional $400 apparently covered costs. It disclaimed an interest in the fund but denied liability. Counsel explained that surrendering a claim to the money did not concede the insured’s negligence and expose the insured to uninsured liability. At least one claimant moved to dismiss.

sections.title: Both interpleader routes have a jurisdictional basis
sections.cue: The claims compete for an inadequate fund
paragraphs: Pan American invoked Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 22 and statutory interpleader under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1335, 1397, and 2361. It was a Texas citizen with its principal business there; Wells was a Wisconsin citizen and the other claimants Louisiana residents. Complete diversity between insurer and claimants supported ordinary diversity jurisdiction for Rule 22. Diversity among claimants supported statutory interpleader, and the fund exceeded the then-applicable ordinary diversity amount and statutory interpleader’s $500 minimum. Judge Wright therefore did not need to settle competing treatments of an interested stakeholder’s citizenship.

Traditional strict interpleader involved a disinterested holder, while a bill in the nature of interpleader could involve contested claims. Modern rule and statute allowed both. Exposure to multiple litigation over one insufficient fund supplied equitable justification without an additional special ground. Merely facing unrelated suits or demands below coverage would not suffice.

A policy cap did not defeat potential multiple liability; the possibility of excessive payment was enough. Different amounts or legal sources did not remove adversity, because each recovery reduced the money available for others.

sections.title: Tort uncertainty and equitable labels do not bar the action
sections.cue: The court preserves trial of legal issues
paragraphs: The court rejected unclean hands. Louisiana’s description of insurer and insured as joint tortfeasors served prescription rules and did not establish that Pan American caused the accident. The insured’s own wrong and unlimited liability raised different concerns but did not defeat this insurer’s request.

The tort claims need not already be liquidated judgments. Four deaths and many injuries reasonably supported anticipating claims over $100,000, and Louisiana direct-action law allowed claims against the insurer without prior judgments against its insured. Equitable interpleader also need not eliminate jury rights: negligence and damages could go to a jury, with the court retaining allocation of an inadequate fund under separate-issue procedures.

sections.title: Statutory interpleader supplies the necessary procedure
sections.cue: The insurer remains while claims are adjudicated
paragraphs: Section 2361 expressly authorized injunctions within the Anti-Injunction Act’s exception for congressional authorization. Rule 22 alone lacked that express power. Wright favored, while acknowledging doubt about, a possible injunction under the separate necessary-in-aid-of-jurisdiction exception, but the actual decree rested on statutory interpleader.

That route also mattered for the venue and service rules then applicable. Wells’s Wisconsin citizenship prevented a common defendant-residence venue in Louisiana under Rule 22, leaving the insurer’s Texas domicile, with service ordinarily confined to the forum state. Statutory interpleader allowed venue where a claimant lived and nationwide service. Without Wells’s waiver and appearance or Louisiana presence, only the statute maintained this suit there.

On September 30, 1960, Wright denied dismissal and granted interpleader. Pan American remained a party because it still owed a contractual duty to resist claims. The court directed injunctions against pending and future accident suits against both insurer and insured, required claims by answer within thirty days of notice, provided a joint jury trial on timely demand, and reserved allocation if aggregate verdicts exceeded coverage. It did not decide fault or award compensation.
